newsitem.title: PERU: FEATURE-Peru's Fujimori -- president for life?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Peru's Fujimori -- president for life?.

text.p: Popular again after rescuing 71 hostages alive from under the guns of leftist guerrillas, Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori seems to be setting the stage for a run for a third consecutive term in office.

The elections are three years away in 2000. But with his approval rating at close to 70 percent after the raid on the Japanese ambassador's house, Fujimori has been been talking openly about the possibility of a third term and looking more self-assured and confident as he jets around the country.
"If a small window of opportunity opens up, it could happen," he said in an interview with television channel CBS-Telenoticias, when asked if he wanted to be reelected.

He may not stop there. Some supporters want to change Peru's electoral laws to allow Fujimori to be re-elected indefinitely -- a goal which some say Fujimori is already working towards with Machiavellian zeal.

"There are many Peruvians who want Fujimori to be president-for-life. They look around and ask, who else is there?" said a member of Peru's Congress and Fujimori supporter, who asked not to be identified.
"I think he really has not yet decided whether to run again. He'll prepare the ground now (for re-eelction) but then decide when the time comes whether to go for it," he said.
It is a prospect that has many people nervous in this country with a long tradition of populist, strongarm rulers who straddle the line between dictator and democrat.

With the guerrilla siege behind them, Peruvians seem to be focusing more on what they perceive as Fujimori's shortcomings -- namely, his government's inability to translate one of the world's highest economic growth rates into more jobs and less poverty.
LIFE AFTER TERRORISM

"'El Chino' finished off terrorism and he wants to stay in power forever. But here there is misery and poverty and a lot of unemployment," said Lino Palomino, as he washed cars for tips at a Lima parking lot, using an affectionate nickname for Fujimori. It means literally The Chinaman.
Critics say Fujimori, known for his tough-guy tactics with opponents and success in crushing leftist guerrilla violence, is moving subtly to discourage any viable challengers.

"He has surrounded himself with people who can be easily discarded so there will be no one in his government to threaten him or replace him in 2000," said Fernando Rospigliosi, a local political columnist.
"His early days when he hired talented people for his Cabinet like (economy ministers) Juan Carlos Hurtado Miller and Carlos Bolona are over. Now he wants discardable types," said Rospigliosi.

The government is full of bland technocrats, he said. His nearest rival in the polls, Lima Mayor Alberto Andrade, accuses Fujimori of deliberately trying to make him look bad by withdrawing police forces during street disturbances last month in the city centre.

First elected to a five-year term in 1990 and re-elected in 1995 with 64 percent of the vote, Fujimori has won credit for bringing the economy back from the brink of collapse and restoring a measure of faith in government.
LIKED BY BANKERS

He is a favourite of international bankers and investors --ironic for a man who is one of Latin America's few sitting presidents from a truly working-class background. He was raised by Japanese immigrant parents in Lima's hardscrabble La Victoria neighbourhood, and he still has a deep connection with the Peruvian poor that lesser politicians can only envy.
But to seek a third term presents one big problem: the constitution which Fujimori's own government wrote in 1992 allows only a single successive reelection, which he won in 1995.

So his supporters press Peru's National Elections Board to accept an interpretation of the law which holds that since the constitution took effect in 1993, Fujimori's first election does not count. Therefore, the single reelection would be the one in 2000.
His opponents have challenged the effort in court, calling it an obvious ploy to bend the rules in favour of one person, and may succeed in turning the whole issue over to a referendum.
Or Fujimori may try to amend the constitution, or he may give the next elections a miss and run instead in 2005, a scenario which the constitution as it stands would allow.
Whichever formula he chooses, few people in Peru think Fujimori, 57, will simply retire from politics in 2000 and go home.

Fujimori reached perhaps his finest moment last month when army and navy commandos swarmed into the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence and freed 71 of the 72 hostages held inside by Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas.
In a country that endured 30,000 deaths from 17 years of guerrilla violence, Fujimori's victory over MRTA may be long forgotten by 2000.

"A year later, people will have completely forgotten about this," said Carlos Ferrero Costa, a member of Fujimori's New Majority-Cambio 90 party in Congress. "Peru has too many problems for people to remember this for very long."
